job: Fresh graduate in computing and engineering
name: Carla Rahman

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello, and thank you. I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and what you say is confidential. So you can tell me the public version and the private one. Tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm doing a master's in structural engineering at Ashford. I still live with my parents, so I take the train in, sit in lectures until two, then do calculations in the library. I like problems with a right answer, where a beam holds or it doesn't. After that I go home and help in my dad's hardware shop for a couple of hours, mostly on the till.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Civil engineering, passed, nothing special. My final project was a design for a footbridge over a drainage canal, and my supervisor said the loads were right but the presentation was dull. I had no internship because the firms I wrote to never answered.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's call this one "AI Plateau". Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine. I'd say what I've always said, which is that new tools come and go. Structures still need a person to sign them off. I wouldn't post anything, I don't really post.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it means nothing changes and I've got to get a job the old way, with a pass degree and no experience. That's hard enough. Bridges and buildings still go up, so there's work, but firms take their time and prefer people they already know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the master's and apply to the three big local consultancies and every council engineering office within an hour of home. I'd go to the careers evening with a printed CV. And I'd carry on at the shop so I'm earning a bit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Steady. It's the world I'm used to, so I'm not frightened by it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why printed CV, not online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because the online forms just swallow them. At the last careers evening I handed my CV to an engineer, Mrs Dalloway, and she remembered my footbridge. A form never remembers my name, but a person standing in front of me might.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What are the pressures you carry in this one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The loan, about 8,500, and the fact that my parents are paying for the master's partly. Dad never says it, but the shop doesn't make much. I feel I'm spending his money while I wait.

say: New tools come and go, and structures still need a **person** to sign them off.
I wouldn't post anything, because I don't really **post**.
think: Nothing changes, so I still need a **job** the old way.
I feel I'm spending my **father's** money while I wait.
do: **Apply** to three big local consultancies and every nearby council engineering office.
Go to the **careers evening** with a printed CV.
Keep helping at the **shop** for pocket money.
feel: **Steady**, because this is the world I'm used to.
S0.quote: A form never remembers my name, but a person standing in front of me might.
fieldNote: Resistant to change, so a plateau fits her **comfort** zone.
Her real stress is **family money**, not technology.
Trusts face-to-face contact over online forms, which she says never remember her name.

steps.text: Apply to three local consultancies and the nearby council engineering offices
Keep working shop shifts on the till for pocket money

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's call this one "Steady Disruption". Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the paperwork side of engineering will change, but bridges don't build themselves. Drawings and calculations could go faster, which means firms might need fewer juniors to produce them. I'd say that to my friends and leave it there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it worries me more. The junior jobs are the calculation checking and drawing, and that's the work software takes first. I've never used the tools and I don't plan to start with them, so I'd be a slow beginner among fast ones.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay on the course and aim at site-based roles, where someone has to walk the ground and check what's built. I'd learn the design software the firms already use, which is boring but proven. And I'd ask the council engineer, Mr Haddad, whether they take trainee site inspectors.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. I can feel it coming, but I haven't got a way to deal with it yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you wouldn't start with the new tools. Can you say why?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't like the answers I can't check. A calculation, I can trace line by line. If I can't trace how a machine got a number for a bridge, I won't put my name under it. That's not stubbornness, it's what the job is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And if the firms demand you use them?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd learn it, slowly, and double-check everything by hand. I'd be the slowest in the office for a while. That's my honest answer, and I think some firms would still want someone careful.

say: Drawings may get **faster**, but bridges don't build themselves.
Firms might need **fewer juniors** to produce the paperwork.
think: Junior **checking** and drawing is the work software takes first.
I'm a **slow beginner** among fast ones with these tools.
do: **Aim** for site-based roles where someone must check what's built.
Learn the **design software** firms already use.
Ask **Mr Haddad** (the council engineer) about trainee site inspectors.
feel: **Uneasy**: I feel it coming without a way to handle it.
S1.quote: If I can't trace how a machine got a number for a bridge, I won't put my name under it.
fieldNote: Her caution is **professional**: she won't sign what she can't trace.
Retreats toward **site work**, which is slower to automate.
Would adopt the tools only under pressure, then **slowly**.

steps.text: Apply for trainee site inspector roles at councils and contractors
Learn the structural design software used by local firms
Ask Mr Haddad for a work shadow day at the council

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's call this one "AGI by 2028". Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that two years is far too quick and the people who make the rules are asleep. I'd ask my MP what the plan is, in a letter, not an email.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be frightened but also stubborn. I don't believe it will go as cleanly as the card says, but if it does, my degree is a bit of paper. I'd have just started work, if I'm lucky.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop any spending that isn't food or transport and keep the shop shifts. I'd look for the sort of work that needs a body on site, like inspection or surveying. And I'd ask Dad whether I could take over some of the shop's ordering, since that's work I understand and he trusts me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tight in the chest. I'd keep it to myself at dinner so Mum doesn't worry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is the shop a plan or a hiding place?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit of both. A hardware shop in a small town sells nails and paint, and robots would come to that later. I'd be a structural engineer behind a till, and I'd rather that than a graduate with no income at all. It's not the dream, but it keeps the lights on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your parents?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them straight that I may not make the money back on the master's. Mum would say we'll manage. Dad would go quiet and then offer me more shifts. That's how he says it.

say: Two years is **too quick**, and rule-makers are asleep.
I'd write my **MP** a letter and ask for the plan.
think: If it goes as described, my **degree** is a piece of paper.
I'm **frightened** but stubborn, and I doubt it's this clean.
do: Look for on-site **inspection** or surveying work.
Take over some of the shop's **ordering** from Dad.
feel: **Tight** in the chest, which I'd hide from Mum.
S2.quote: I'd be a structural engineer behind a till, and I'd rather that than a graduate with no income at all.
fieldNote: Resistance leaves her with **few levers**, so she falls back on family.
Won't call the shop a dream, but sees it as **income**.
Hides worry at home to protect her **mother**.

steps.text: Cut spending down to food and train fares
Apply for on-site inspection and surveying jobs
Take over the shop's weekly ordering from Dad
Write a letter to the MP asking for the plan

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's call this one "AGI by 2031". Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is long enough to notice who's ready and who isn't. I'd tell people to be careful with money and not make big commitments while it's unclear.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd manage. I'd finish the master's, get a first job, and have two or three years of experience on site before it lands. That would make me more useful than someone who has only done calculations.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take any engineering job that gets me on site, even if it pays little. I'd save about 200 a month and not move out until the loan is below 5,000. And I'd do one short course on the new tools, only because employers will ask me about them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alright, mostly. There's a weight, but I can carry it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why not move out?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Rent is the biggest cost in my world and it kills savings. Living with my parents is a gift I can pay back later. I'd rather get my loan down by living at home than prove I'm independent with rent I can't afford.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does 'the weight' consist of?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Debt, a pass degree, and knowing that the hiring rules will probably change at the same moment I'm applying. I'm fine as long as I stay organised. If I wobble, the weight wins.

say: Five years is long enough to see who is **ready**.
Be careful with money and avoid **big commitments**.
think: I'd have two or three years on **site** before it lands.
Site experience makes me more **useful** than a calculation-only graduate.
do: **Take** any engineering job that puts me on site.
**Save** 200 a month and stay home until the loan is below 5,000.
Take one short course on the **new tools** because employers will ask.
feel: **Alright**, with a weight I can carry.
S3.quote: I'd rather get my loan down by living at home than prove I'm independent with rent I can't afford.
fieldNote: The caution that holds her back from change also makes her a **careful** saver.
Choosing to **live at home** is a deliberate money plan.
Her mood depends on staying **organised**, and she knows it.

steps.text: Take the first engineering job that puts me on building sites
Save 200 a month while living at home
Take one short course on AI tools for engineers

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's call this one "AGI by 2036". Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty of time to prepare, so there's no excuse for panic. I'd tell friends to study something and put money aside.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I feel nearly normal. By 34 I could be chartered, which is the professional qualification for engineers, and in a job that needs a person on site for years more. Robots for hands-on work come 3 years later still.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd work toward chartered status over the next five years, buy a small flat with my savings, and stay in site-based work. I'd read a bit about the new tools each year, just to know what the firms are using.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. It's the first one where my own life looks pretty much normal.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the chartered status give you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A title that means a person has been examined and can take responsibility. When something goes wrong with a building, the law wants a person's name on it, not a program's name. That feels safer than any skill with a trend attached.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Anything that could spoil the calm?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the changes arrive faster than the card says, or if my parents' shop closes. Dad's shop is the real worry, because we'd all feel it. I don't think AI is what would close it, but a big chain might.

say: Ten years is **plenty** of time, so no excuse for panic.
Study something useful and **put money aside** while the decade lasts.
think: By 34 I could be **chartered** and on site for years more.
Law wants a **person's name** on a building, not a program's.
do: **Work toward** chartered engineer status over five years.
**Buy** a small flat with my savings.
**Read** about new tools each year to see what firms use.
feel: **Calm**: my life looks mostly normal here.
S4.quote: When something goes wrong with a building, the law wants a person's name on it, not a program's name.
fieldNote: The long window suits her **cautious** nature; she can plan.
Her anchor is **legal responsibility**, which needs a person.
The one real worry is her **father's** shop, not AI.

steps.text: Work toward chartered engineer status over five years
Save for a deposit on a small flat
Read about one new engineering tool each year

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one, because I'm the sort who needs time to learn something new. What would help is a clear graduate route into site jobs, and guidance from the engineering institutions about what's changing, in plain words.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe that quiet people have views too. I don't post and I don't shout, but I notice everything, and I know what's holding up the building I'm sitting in.

headlineQuote: I don't post and I don't shout, but I notice everything, and I know what's holding up the building I'm sitting in.
portrait: Carla is 24, doing a **structural engineering** master's after a pass in civil engineering.
She lives with her parents in **Ashford** and helps in her father's hardware shop.
Centrist and cautious, she never uses **AI tools** and distrusts answers she can't trace.
Her shelter is **site-based** work, where a person's name and presence still count.
Her mood runs from uneasy to alarmed, and **family money** is the thread.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** worries her most, because she needs time to learn new things.
whatWouldHelp: A clear **graduate route** into site jobs and plain guidance from engineering institutions.
